meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'It is often said that before you die your life passes before your eyes. It is in fact true. It's called living'?
meta.ogDescription: Pratchett's idea but not his wording. In The Last Continent (1998), Death tells Rincewind that the process is called 'living.' The popular version is a paraphrase.

answer.label: Not Terry Pratchett’s wording — a paraphrase of The Last Continent
answer.authorDates: 1948–2015 · English author of the Discworld novels
answer.sourceLine: The idea really is Pratchett’s. In The Last Continent (1998), Death tells Rincewind that people’s whole lives do pass in front of their eyes before they die, and that “the process is called ‘living.’” The neat three-sentence version that circulates is a later paraphrase, not the book’s text, and Wikiquote flags it as one ↗.

source.heading: Where the line really comes from
source.excerpt:
“Is it true that your life passes before your eyes before you die?”
YES.
“Ghastly thought, really.” Rincewind shuddered. “Oh gods, I’ve just had another one. Suppose I am just about to die and this is my whole life passing in front of my eyes?”
I THINK PERHAPS YOU DO NOT UNDERSTAND. PEOPLE’S WHOLE LIVES DO PASS IN FRONT OF THEIR EYES BEFORE THEY DIE. THE PROCESS IS CALLED “LIVING.”
trail: 1998 — Doubleday in London publishes The Last Continent, the 22nd Discworld novel (Wikipedia ↗).

In the novel, Rincewind asks whether your life passes before your eyes before you die, and Death answers that people’s whole lives do pass in front of their eyes and that “the process is called ‘living’” (Wikiquote transcription, p. 260 ↗; the passage also appears in the Internet Archive’s scan of the 1999 US edition ↗).
2008 — The compressed version, “… It is in fact true. It’s called living,” is in print credited to “Terry Pratchett” in a devotional journal (Internet Archive ↗).
Wikiquote lists the popular version on its Terry Pratchett page with the note that “this popular quote seems to be a paraphrase of an exchange in The Last Continent” (Wikiquote ↗).
source.cutTag: ↑ Pratchett’s actual words. “It is often said … It’s called living” is a paraphrase
source.excerptNote: Death’s lines are printed in capitals in the novel. The quotation marks around “living” vary between editions. The transcription follows Wikiquote’s Discworld page ↗, which cites the 2000 HarperTorch mass-market paperback, p. 260. The opening “It is often said” and the closing “It’s called living” are not the book’s words.

author.name: Terry Pratchett
author.heading: Terry Pratchett
author.bio: Sir Terry Pratchett (1948–2015) was an English author best known for the 41-novel Discworld series. The Last Continent (1998), the 22nd Discworld novel and the sixth to star the cowardly wizard Rincewind, contains the exchange with Death that this popular line paraphrases. In the novel the line is spoken by the character Death. It is not Pratchett speaking in his own voice.

misattribution.heading: How the line drifted
misattribution.intro: Pratchett’s idea survives, but the words people share are not the ones he printed. The line has been tidied into an aphorism and attached to his name as if it were a direct quotation.

items.who: Terry Pratchett, as a direct quote
items.why: Quote sites present “It is often said that before you die your life passes before your eyes. It is, in fact, true. It’s called living” as Pratchett’s words, some of them crediting The Last Continent (Goodreads ↗). In the novel, though, Death says something different: “The process is called ‘living’” (Wikiquote ↗).

By 2008 the compressed version was in print credited to “Terry Pratchett” (devotional journal, 2008 ↗). A shorter one-liner, “Before you die your life passes before your eyes – it’s called living,” appears in a 2005 joke collection (Internet Archive ↗).

items.who: “… That is true, it’s called Life”
items.why: A further variant swaps “living” for “Life.” WIST lists it as a paraphrase alongside the genuine passage from The Last Continent (WIST ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The thought belongs to Pratchett’s Death in The Last Continent (1998): “People’s whole lives do pass in front of their eyes before they die. The process is called ‘living.’” The popular wording is a paraphrase (Wikiquote ↗).

context.heading: Why the line works
lead: The exchange is a typical Pratchett reversal. Rincewind, who spends most of the Discworld books running away from danger, worries that this very moment might be his life flashing before his eyes. Death takes the old cliché literally and turns it into a remark about life itself.

Because the aphorism keeps the joke and drops the setting, it reads like a stand-alone saying. That made it easy to repeat, and easy to reword. The version people share is shorter and tidier than the book’s, but the point and the punchline are Pratchett’s.
